title: Rapid, concerted switching of the neural code in inferotemporal cortex
abstract: A fundamental paradigm in neuroscience is the concept of neural coding through tuning functions <sup>1</sup> . According to this idea, neurons encode stimuli through fixed mappings of stimulus features to firing rates. Here, we report that the tuning of visual neurons can rapidly and coherently change across a population to attend to a whole and its parts. We set out to investigate a longstanding debate concerning whether inferotemporal (IT) cortex uses a specialized code for representing specific types of objects or whether it uses a general code that applies to any object. We found that face cells in macaque IT cortex initially adopted a general code optimized for face detection. But following a rapid, concerted population event lasting < 20 ms, the neural code transformed into a face-specific one with two striking properties: (i) response gradients to principal detection-related dimensions reversed direction, and (ii) new tuning developed to multiple higher feature space dimensions supporting fine face discrimination. These dynamics were face specific and did not occur in response to objects. Overall, these results show that, for faces, face cells shift from detection to discrimination by switching from an object-general code to a face-specific code. More broadly, our results suggest a novel mechanism for neural representation: concerted, stimulus-dependent switching of the neural code used by a cortical area.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This bioRxiv preprint has already drawn measurable scholarly attention, with 14 OpenAlex citations, 12 scite citation statements, and 16 documented downstream reuse instances. Its citation trail is especially notable for how quickly it accumulated, with most citing works appearing in 2025 and 2026, and for the breadth of venues engaging with the work, including high-profile journals and reviews in neuroscience and related fields.

Full narrative

Shi and colleagues challenge a core assumption in neuroscience by arguing that inferotemporal cortex can rapidly and coherently switch its neural code across a population, rather than relying on fixed tuning alone. That premise has resonated with subsequent research: the paper has 14 citations in OpenAlex, and the citing record shows early and sustained uptake after its 2023 posting. The response is not confined to preprints; the work is also cited in peer-reviewed articles and reviews, suggesting that it has begun to shape both active research and synthesis in the field.

The downstream literature points to a particularly strong fit with work on visual cortex, neural dynamics, and object and face perception. Recent citing papers include studies in Science, Nature, PLoS Biology, and the Journal of Neuroscience, alongside additional bioRxiv preprints. Several of these citations come from research on human and macaque visual systems, indicating that the article’s central ideas about flexible coding and population-level representation are being taken up across closely related lines of inquiry rather than remaining isolated to one subtopic.

The reuse signals reinforce that pattern. In addition to citation activity, the work appears in 16 documented reuse instances, including two Europe PMC article mentions and reuse by a mix of preprints, articles, and a review. Scite also records four supporting citation statements, which adds another layer of evidence that later authors are citing the paper in an affirming or building-on manner. Taken together, these signals suggest that the article is not only being noticed, but is being used as part of the conceptual framework for ongoing work on neural coding.

The broader attention record is comparatively quiet outside scholarly channels: event data and public discourse signals are limited in the digest, so the strongest evidence is clearly academic rather than general-audience reach. Even so, the combination of rapid citations, reuse in multiple work types, and uptake in prominent neuroscience venues indicates a paper that has quickly entered the conversation around how visual information is encoded and transformed in inferotemporal cortex.
